description: Test your knowledge of Features of individual bones (Upper Limb) — clavicle and scapula anatomy, muscle attachments, and clinical correlations for MBBS.

cards.text: How do you determine the side of a clavicle bone? Describe the key anatomical features.
cards.answer: Medial end is rounded (sternoclavicular articulation); lateral end is flat (acromioclavicular articulation). Medial two-thirds convex anteriorly; lateral one-third concave anteriorly (S-shape from above). Conoid tubercle and trapezoid ridge at lateral end (inferior surface).

tip.tip: MEdial = rounded (like a sternum socket); LAteral = flat (like acromion). Convex-Concave = S-shaped curve.

cards.text: What is the most common fracture site of the clavicle? What happens to each fragment?
cards.answer: Junction of medial two-thirds and lateral one-third (weakest point). Medial fragment pulled upward by sternocleidomastoid; lateral fragment drops due to weight of arm and gravity.

tip.tip: Medial fragment UP (SCM pulls); lateral fragment DOWN (gravity pulls). Think of a broken bridge: inner end up, outer end down.

cards.text: Name the five key muscles attached to the clavicle and their actions.
cards.answer: Sternocleidomastoid (medial, rotates head); trapezius (lateral-posterior, elevates shoulder); deltoid (lateral-anterior, abducts arm); pectoralis major (medial-anterior, adducts/flexes); subclavius (inferior groove, depresses clavicle).

tip.tip: STernocleidomastoid, TRapezius, DEltoid, PEctoralis, SUbclavius = STDEPS (for Shoulder Dynamics).

cards.text: What are the two structures on the inferior surface of the clavicle, and what do they protect/attach?
cards.answer: Subclavian groove (medial) protects subclavius muscle and underlying subclavian vessels/brachial plexus. Conoid tubercle and trapezoid ridge (lateral) attach the coracoclavicular ligament, which suspends the scapula.

tip.tip: SUbclavian groove = SUbclavius muscle inside; ConoId tubercle = coracoclavicular ligament. Protection = vessels/plexus underneath.

cards.text: Describe the scapula's three surfaces and their main features.
cards.answer: Costal (anterior): subscapular fossa (subscapularis origin). Posterior (dorsal): spine divides into supraspinous fossa (supraspinatus origin) and infraspinous fossa (infraspinatus origin). Lateral angle bears glenoid cavity for glenohumeral joint.

tip.tip: Costal = subscapularis (inside hollow). Posterior = spine splits fossae: SUpra (above) and INfra (below). Lateral = glenoid (ball socket).

cards.text: What are the two main processes of the scapula and their key attachments?
cards.answer: Spine of scapula (posterior, continues as acromion laterally — shoulder roof). Coracoid process (anterior hook at superior angle) — attaches short head of biceps, coracobrachialis, pectoralis minor, and coracoclavicular ligament.

tip.tip: Spine = roof over shoulder (acromion). Coracoid = hooked beak (coraco- = raven/crow) with biceps hanging from it.

cards.text: Which muscle origin is associated with 'winging of the scapula' when paralysed? What nerve is damaged?
cards.answer: Serratus anterior (attaches to medial and inferior borders of scapula, 'boxer's muscle'). Long thoracic nerve injury causes winging — the medial border protrudes posteriorly due to loss of protraction.

tip.tip: SEratus ANterior (SEAN) = Boxer's punch. Paralysis = Winged scapula (looks like pterodactyl wing sticking out). Long thoracic = injury from axilla dissection/trauma.

cards.text: Name the three rotator cuff muscles and their origins on the scapula.
cards.answer: Supraspinatus (supraspinous fossa, initiates abduction); infraspinatus (infraspinous fossa, lateral rotation); teres minor (lateral border of infraspinous fossa, lateral rotation). All stabilize glenohumeral joint and prevent anterior dislocation.

tip.tip: SUPRA-infra SPINOUS fossae = SUPRa and INFRa. Teres = round, minor = smaller. SPIT = Stabilize (rotator cuff), Prevent Impingement, medial/Lateral rotation.
